metric.why: Announced megawatts are the leading indicator for land, power, and equipment demand. The published numbers come almost entirely from commercial research firms; this site links to who publishes them rather than republishing figures it cannot verify.
metric.definition: Capacity in permitting, planned, or under construction per market, the standard unit for comparing data center booms across regions.

reading.body:
Announced megawatts in the construction pipeline are the leading indicator for where AI infrastructure will physically concentrate, what cities will bear its power demands, and which regions will capture its economic effects.

Data centers exist only as announced projects before they exist at all. The pipeline metric tracks capacity in permitting, planning, or active construction across markets. This reveals which geographies are positioning themselves for AI scaling before the facilities draw power or house equipment. Because announced capacity typically precedes energized capacity by years, these figures show the trajectory of regional infrastructure commitment and competition.

For AI specifically, the construction pipeline matters because compute cannot exceed what the grid and buildings can supply. A region with aggressive pipeline growth is signaling it expects to compete for AI workloads. Conversely, regions with modest announcements may face binding constraints on AI deployment even if they have other advantages. The megawatt unit makes different projects and regions directly comparable, moving past vague claims about expansion.

This metric does not capture whether announced projects will actually be built, when they will come online, or how much power will actually be consumed once operational. It reflects what companies have publicly announced, not what will ultimately be constructed or delivered to the grid. Market conditions, permitting delays, or power availability can narrow the gap between announced and realized capacity.
